ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: A no-code graphical Builder lowers the barrier to experiment authoring while preserving full parameter-level configurability for researchers who require it; results are collected as encrypted payloads with multi-factor authentication gating and pseudonymised participant linkage, supporting compliance with GDPR, UK GDPR, and IRB data management requirements.

Production-grade security measures -including Fernet-symmetric payload encryption, salted SHA-256 participant pseudonymisation, MFA-gated decrypt access, and immutable audit logging -are built into the platform codebase rather than delegated to institutional infrastructure, designed to support compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), UK GDPR, and Institutional Review Board (IRB) data management expectations out of the box.

CogFlow's security model is designed around the recognition that participant behavioural data constitutes sensitive research output subject to institutional ethical oversight, and that a platform intended for broad adoption across research groups must provide technically credible data-protection controls that can be directly cited in ethics board submissions and data management plans.
table.header: 3 Security Measures Ensuring Confidentiality and Safety of Data Transmission

table.text: The platform's compliance posture is designed to be consistent with the requirements of major research data-governance frameworks, including GDPR (EU 2016/679), UK GDPR, IRB data management plan expectations, and Australian data governance frameworks, with the Ethics and Compliance module inside the researcher portal providing copy-ready paragraphs mapped to specific data-protection dimensions for direct use in ethics board submissions.

table.text: The platform integrates 1 natively with SONA Systems and Prolific Academic for participant recruitment, provides in-portal descriptive analysis and charting, and includes a CogFlow To Go packaging mode for offline laboratory deployment with Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) support for physiological co-registration.

Native integrations with SONA Systems and Prolific Academic streamline participant recruitment; an in-portal Analysis module provides preliminary descriptive reporting and charting before data are downloaded; and a CogFlow To Go packaging mode enables offline laboratory deployment with Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) support, extending the same study configurations to settings that require physiological co-registration or guaranteed network independence.

4 "Recruitment" refers to built-in support for linking studies with participant recruitment systems such as SONA, Prolific, or MTurk, rather than recruitment through independently configured external workflows.

CogFlow integrates natively with two of the most widely used participant recruitment platforms in academic cognitive psychology research, SONA Systems and Prolific Academic, via a dedicated Integrations module in the researcher portal (Figure 5).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

ethics_statements: A no-code graphical Builder lowers the barrier to experiment authoring while preserving full parameter-level configurability for researchers who require it; results are collected as encrypted payloads with multi-factor authentication gating and pseudonymised participant linkage, supporting compliance with GDPR, UK GDPR, and IRB data management requirements.

Production-grade security measures -including Fernet-symmetric payload encryption, salted SHA-256 participant pseudonymisation, MFA-gated decrypt access, and immutable audit logging -are built into the platform codebase rather than delegated to institutional infrastructure, designed to support compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), UK GDPR, and Institutional Review Board (IRB) data management expectations out of the box.

CogFlow's security model is designed around the recognition that participant behavioural data constitutes sensitive research output subject to institutional ethical oversight, and that a platform intended for broad adoption across research groups must provide technically credible data-protection controls that can be directly cited in ethics board submissions and data management plans.

The platform's compliance posture is designed to be consistent with the requirements of major research data-governance frameworks, including GDPR (EU 2016/679), UK GDPR, IRB data management plan expectations, and Australian data governance frameworks, with the Ethics and Compliance module inside the researcher portal providing copy-ready paragraphs mapped to specific data-protection dimensions for direct use in ethics board submissions.
live_data_statements: The platform integrates 1 natively with SONA Systems and Prolific Academic for participant recruitment, provides in-portal descriptive analysis and charting, and includes a CogFlow To Go packaging mode for offline laboratory deployment with Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) support for physiological co-registration.

Native integrations with SONA Systems and Prolific Academic streamline participant recruitment; an in-portal Analysis module provides preliminary descriptive reporting and charting before data are downloaded; and a CogFlow To Go packaging mode enables offline laboratory deployment with Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) support, extending the same study configurations to settings that require physiological co-registration or guaranteed network independence.

4 "Recruitment" refers to built-in support for linking studies with participant recruitment systems such as SONA, Prolific, or MTurk, rather than recruitment through independently configured external workflows.

CogFlow integrates natively with two of the most widely used participant recruitment platforms in academic cognitive psychology research, SONA Systems and Prolific Academic, via a dedicated Integrations module in the researcher portal (Figure 5).

For Prolific Academic, the portal generates an external study URL that embeds the standard Prolific URL parameters ({{PROLIFIC PID}}, {{STUDY ID}}, and {{SESSION ID}}), with configurable completion behaviour set to auto-redirect to the Prolific completion page by default.

A researcher designs a task in the Builder, validates its timing and logic, and publishes it, which creates a study record together with its first configuration version; the resulting participant link can then be distributed directly or routed through a recruitment pipeline such as Prolific.
No experiments involving human participants were conducted, and nothing was preregistered.

text.text: Proliferating web-based experimentation platforms have substantially broadened access to cognitive psychology research infrastructure, yet no existing tool simultaneously supports continuous and trial-based paradigms, maintains institutional data-protection compliance, works across online and laboratory settings, and operates within the constraints of collaborative multi-site teams.
We present CogFlow, a free, open-source, self-hostable web platform for constructing, deploying, and managing cognitive psychology experiments.

CogFlow's JSONcentric architecture uses a single declarative configuration file to specify both study design and runtime instructions for the Interpreter engine, supporting a broad task library including Random Dot Motion, Flanker, SART, Stroop and Emotional Stroop, Simon, Task Switching, PVT, MOT, N-back, Gabor patch, Continuous Image Presentation, and Security Operations Centre (SOC)-style multitask environments, in both trial-based and continuous-presentation modes.

A no-code graphical Builder lowers the barrier to experiment authoring while preserving full parameter-level configurability for researchers who require it; results are collected as encrypted payloads with multi-factor authentication gating and pseudonymised participant linkage, supporting compliance with GDPR, UK GDPR, and IRB data management requirements.

The platform integrates 1 natively with SONA Systems and Prolific Academic for participant recruitment, provides in-portal descriptive analysis and charting, and includes a CogFlow To Go packaging mode for offline laboratory deployment with Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) support for physiological co-registration.
Software-layer runtime benchmarks confirm stable performance consistent with the broader literature on browser-based platforms.
CogFlow is available at https://cogflow.app under the BSD 3-Clause licence; contributor roles are tracked using the CRediT taxonomy with versioned archival via Zenodo.
text.formatted: CogFlow is available at <ref type="url" target="https://cogflow.app">https://cogflow.app</ref> under the BSD 3-Clause licence; contributor roles are tracked using the CRediT taxonomy with versioned archival via Zenodo.

text.text: The design and delivery of cognitive psychology experiments increasingly takes place in web-based environments, a shift accelerated by the practical demands of largescale online data collection and the recognised advantages of browser-delivered stimuli for accessibility, sample diversity, and replication across sites (e.g., Bridges, Pitiot, MacAskill, & Peirce, 2020).
text.formatted: The design and delivery of cognitive psychology experiments increasingly takes place in web-based environments, a shift accelerated by the practical demands of largescale online data collection and the recognised advantages of browser-delivered stimuli for accessibility, sample diversity, and replication across sites (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bridges, Pitiot, MacAskill, & Peirce, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A range of platforms now exists to support this workflow, from full-featured desktop solutions with online export pathways such as PsychoPy and Pavlovia (Peirce et al., 2019) to browser-native frameworks including jsPsych (de Leeuw, Gilbert, & Luchterhandt, 2023) and lab.js (Henninger, Shevchenko, Mertens, Kieslich, & Hilbig, 2022), and server-managed experiment management systems such as JATOS (Lange, Kühn, & Filevich, 2015).
text.formatted: A range of platforms now exists to support this workflow, from full-featured desktop solutions with online export pathways such as PsychoPy and Pavlovia <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Peirce et al., 2019)</ref> to browser-native frameworks including jsPsych (de <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Leeuw, Gilbert, & Luchterhandt, 2023)</ref> and lab.js <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Henninger, Shevchenko, Mertens, Kieslich, & Hilbig, 2022)</ref>, and server-managed experiment management systems such as JATOS <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Lange, Kühn, & Filevich, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these tools has contributed meaningfully to the methodological infrastructure of the field, yet none addresses the complete set of requirements that characterises modern cognitive research programmes operating at institutional scale.
Specifically, several gaps remain underserved across existing platforms when they are considered individually.

No-code authoring environments typically sacrifice configurability, while fully code-based frameworks require programming competence that not all research teams possess, particularly in supervisory or multi-investigator contexts.

Participant recruitment integrations, in-platform data inspection, and offline laboratory deployment with physiological co-registration are each addressed by separate tools or custom workflows, fragmenting the research pipeline and increasing the technical overhead associated with each new study.

Data security and institutional compliance infrastructure is frequently left to the researcher or their IT department to arrange independently, creating variable and often undocumented data-protection practices across studies.

And while open-source licensing is common, sustainable collaborative attribution frameworks that allow contributors -whether co-investigators, research assistants, or external developers -to formally claim and cite their roles in platform development remain rare.
CogFlow (see Figure 1) was designed to address these gaps within a single, coherent, free-to-use platform.
text.formatted: CogFlow (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>) was designed to address these gaps within a single, coherent, free-to-use platform.

text.text: Its architecture is organised around a JSON-centric core in which a single declarative configuration file serves simultaneously as the humanreadable specification of a study and the runtime instruction set for the Interpreter engine, while participant results are returned in a separate JSON container whose payload is encrypted at ingestion.
This design improves replicability, facilitates preregistration alignment, and keeps deployment lightweight.

A no-code graphical Builder supports experiment authoring across a broad paradigm library, with explicit support for both trial-based and continuous presentation modes and granular parameter control at the block level; researchers with programming expertise can inspect and modify the underlying JSON directly, preserving ultimate flexibility without imposing it as a requirement.

Production-grade security measures -including Fernet-symmetric payload encryption, salted SHA-256 participant pseudonymisation, MFA-gated decrypt access, and immutable audit logging -are built into the platform codebase rather than delegated to institutional infrastructure, designed to support compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), UK GDPR, and Institutional Review Board (IRB) data management expectations out of the box.

Native integrations with SONA Systems and Prolific Academic streamline participant recruitment; an in-portal Analysis module provides preliminary descriptive reporting and charting before data are downloaded; and a CogFlow To Go packaging mode enables offline laboratory deployment with Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) support, extending the same study configurations to settings that require physiological co-registration or guaranteed network independence.
The platform is free to use in perpetuity, self-hostable for institutions requiring data sovereignty, and supported with a documented response commitment for researcher queries.
This paper introduces the CogFlow platform to the cognitive psychology research community, available publicly at https://cogflow.app.
text.formatted: This paper introduces the CogFlow platform to the cognitive psychology research community, available publicly at <ref type="url" target="https://cogflow.app">https://cogflow.app</ref>.

text.text: Here, our focus is the design features of the CogFlow platform rather than a tutorial describing use cases of the platform; the latter is available at a dedicated and up-to-date section of the CogFlow website.
To foreshadow the motivating design features of CogFlow, Table 1 provides a feature-level comparison with representative extant platforms.
text.formatted: To foreshadow the motivating design features of CogFlow, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> provides a feature-level comparison with representative extant platforms.

text.text: Existing platforms provide many of the individual capabilities implemented in CogFlow, but differ in how these capabilities are combined and in the extent to which they form part of an integrated research workflow.
Rather than being distinguished by any single capability, CogFlow is distinguished instead by the intersection of features that are typically distributed across different experimental workflows.

In particular, it brings experiment authoring and deployment together with data management, recruitment, laboratory use, analysis, security, and collaborative research infrastructure within a single platform.
The paper is structured as follows.

We first describe the JSON-centric architecture that underlies the platform's design (2.1), the Builder authoring environment (2.2), the Interpreter engine and its support for standard and bespoke paradigms (2.3), the in-portal Analysis module (2.4), participant recruitment integrations (2.5), CogFlow To Go offline deployment mode (2.6), and the security and compliance infrastructure (3).

We report software-layer runtime benchmarks characterising the platform's timing performance across network conditions (4), user roles and associated privileges (5), and platform availability and contributions (6).
We close with a discussion of current scope, planned development, and the platform's position relative to existing tools (7).

The JSON format occupies a central and load-bearing role throughout the CogFlow architecture, serving simultaneously as the medium for experiment specification, runtime instruction, and participant data capture.

During study design and timeline construction, CogFlow Builder exports a structured JSON configuration object that encodes every parameter required to instantiate a study: top-level fields for experiment type (trial-based or continuous), task scope, data-collection toggles, and UI settings, together with a timeline array that composes individual components, generative Block definitions, structural loop markers, and randomisation-range markers into a complete, declarative description of a session.

This JSON config file is open to sharing and redistributing both for ease of collaboration and for enhancing transparency and replicability of studies: by importing a JSON into a new study, a researcher can easily run a separate iteration of the same paradigm on a separate set of participants.

The config is therefore the single artefact that moves from researcher intent to live deployment -it is published to the platform backend, versioned as a ConfigVersion record, and later retrieved by the Interpreter engine to compile the jsPsych timeline without any further researcher intervention.

On the data-collection side, the JSON file format also plays the central role: at the close of each participant run, the Interpreter assembles a result payload, also in JSON format, that carries the full trial-level behavioural record -response times, accuracy flags, stimulus metadata, and any task-specific fields such as gaze samples -and transmits that payload to the backend via a dedicated submission endpoint.

Critically, the raw payload is not stored in plain text; it is encrypted server-side at the point of ingestion, so the JSON object that enters durable storage is an encrypted envelope whose plain text is inaccessible without an authenticated, MFA-verified decrypt operation.

2 "Ready paradigms" refers to complete or near-complete implementations of cognitive tasks that can be deployed or adapted, rather than lower-level components or plugins used to construct experiments.
3 "Online management" refers to integrated hosting of deployed experiments and server-side management of participant data within the platform or its associated ecosystem.

4 "Recruitment" refers to built-in support for linking studies with participant recruitment systems such as SONA, Prolific, or MTurk, rather than recruitment through independently configured external workflows.
5 "Lab deployment" refers to support for running experiments locally or offline rather than requiring access to the platform's online service.
Native physiological integration is noted where applicable.
6 "Custom code" refers to the capacity to write and integrate bespoke experiment code beyond configuration of predefined tasks or components.
7 "Analysis" refers to facilities within the platform for analysing or visually inspecting collected participant data, rather than analysis performed only after export to external software.

"Security/compliance" refers to data-protection or research-governance infrastructure implemented as an explicit feature of the platform, such as encryption, access controls, audit mechanisms, or documented support for applicable privacy and research-governance requirements.
A cross does not imply that a platform is insecure; it indicates that such infrastructure is not provided as an integrated platform feature.

This design places JSON at the intersection of three architectural concernsstudy specification, runtime execution, and secure data stewardship -and means that any researcher familiar with JSON can inspect, validate, or version-control their study definitions with ordinary text tooling, while the confidentiality of participant data is protected independently of that transparency.
The Builder supports the construction of both trial-based and continuous paradigms using a visual, component-based authoring environment (an example of the UI viewport can be seen on Figure 2).

text.formatted: Experiments are assembled by adding configurable components (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2C</ref>) to a graphical timeline (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2D</ref>) representing the sequence of events within the experiment.

text.text: Components can be reordered, grouped, and nested within experimental blocks, allowing researchers to construct complex task structures without custom programming.

A task-scoped component library provides elements for stimuli, responses, feedback, breaks, surveys, randomisation, loops, save checkpoints, secondary tasks, and thought probes, while complete study configurations are stored as JSONs that can be exported, versioned, reloaded, or published directly to the CogFlow platform.

Researchers may begin from existing task templates or construct paradigms from individual components while retaining parameter-level control over stimulus properties, response modalities, timing, and block structure.
The Builder supports continuous stimulus presentation within the same visual authoring environment used for trial-based paradigms.

For instance, the Builder encodes the random dot motion task in both its canonical discrete-trials format (one response per trial, categorising stimulus identity) and a novel continuous-display format (multiple responses on the basis of changes in stimulus identity).

In both trial formats, researchers can configure all aspects of the random dot motion stimulus through the interface, including coherence, motion direction, dot lifetime, speed, dot density, colour, noise characteristics, and the properties of two independently configurable dot groups, without requiring custom programming.

The Builder therefore provides a common authoring environment across paradigms that differ substantially in experimental structure and appearance, including continuous tasks, discrete trialbased tasks, secondary or auxiliary tasks, questionnaires, and thought probes, all constructed using the same component-based interface, allowing these elements to be combined within a single experimental configuration.
The Builder also supports experimental components that operate independently of the primary task structure.

Secondary tasks, including Detection Response Tasks (DRTs), can be configured to begin and end at predefined points within an experiment, allowing them to operate continuously across multiple task blocks.

Similarly, thought probes, such as those used in the study of task-unrelated thoughts, can be scheduled at configurable intervals independently of task events, while questionnaires may be inserted at any point within the experimental workflow.
Loop and randomisation controls are implemented directly within the timeline, allowing sections of an experiment to be repeated or shuffled without duplicating components.
Configurable save checkpoints preserve participant data throughout an experiment, reducing data loss resulting from participant attrition or unexpected interruptions during online testing.

Completed studies can be previewed before deployment, and published configurations can subsequently be reloaded and modified without reconstructing the experiment, supporting rapid iteration throughout the development process.

The CogFlow Interpreter is a self-contained, browser-side JavaScript runtime that consumes a Builder-exported JSON configuration and compiles it into an executable jsPsych timeline, orchestrating the full sequence of stimulus presentation, response capture, and data submission without requiring any server-side rendering or real-time backend involvement during the experiment itself.

The engine is organised as a small set of loosely coupled JavaScript modules: • configLoader.js handles the resolution of experiment configurations from multiple possible sources (the platform's Django backend, a Cloudflare-hosted Token Store, a local file system via URL parameters, or a direct file-upload fallback); • timelineCompiler.js is the primary compilation engine, traversing the JSON timeline array and expanding each item -standard jsPsych components, generative Blocks, loop-marker pairs, and randomisation-group pairs -into concrete jsPsych trial objects; and • main.js provides the top-level orchestration that sequences loading, compilation, execution, and result submission.

Each cognitive task is implemented as a self-contained jsPsych plugin (e.g., jspsych-rdm.js, jspsych-sart.js, jspsych-gabor.js, jspsych-stroop.js, jspsych-pvt.js, jspsych-nback.js, jspsych-mot.js, jspsych-task-switching.js), loaded as browser globals and consumed by the compiler purely by type key.

This architectural pattern means that new paradigms can be added by supplying a new plugin file and registering its type key in the compiler, without modifying any of the core loading or submission infrastructure, conferring a high degree of extensibility and making the Interpreter straightforwardly portable to institutional servers, JATOS deployments, or standalone hosting environments without modification to its JavaScript source.

In addition to the engine run outside of the main portal interface when delivered straight to participants, the CogFlow portal also allows a Preview of any published study in a dedicated space, as seen in Figure 3.

text.text: Beyond the standard trial-based compilation path, the Interpreter includes dedicated engines for bespoke continuous paradigms that cannot be adequately captured by a simple per-trial compilation loop.
Among such paradigms are tasks like the security operations centre (SOC) Dashboard and Continuous Image Presentation (CIP).

The SOC Dashboard (jspsych-soc-dashboard.js) renders a simulated multiwindow "security operations centre" desktop environment as a single extended jsPsych session, within which up to four simultaneous subtask windows -each implementing a distinct cognitive demand modelled on sustained attention to response (SART), N-back, Flanker, Wisconsin card sorting test (WCST), or psychomotor vigilance task (PVT) paradigms -can be scheduled to appear, overlap temporally, and dismiss according to researcher-specified timing parameters.

All trial-level events from all active subtasks are written into a unified, timestamped events array in real time, giving researchers a fine-grained behavioural record that preserves the temporal relationships among concurrent task demands.

Continuous Image Presentation paradigm similarly uses a purpose-built plugin (jspsych-continuous-image-presentation.js) that sequences a list of assetbacked images with configurable durations and sprite-based masking transitions, compiled from block-level parameter values that the Builder resolves to fully-qualified asset URLs at export time.

For continuous-mode tasks generally, the compiler converts researcher-specified block durations in seconds into frame counts using the experiment-defined frame rate, ensuring that timing is preserved independently of trial-count parameterisation.

Together, these purpose-built engines coexist with the general-purpose plugin architecture without introducing coupling, so the modularity of the codebase is not compromised by the complexity of the paradigms it supports.
CogFlow includes a built-in Analysis module within the researcher portal that is designed to support rapid, in-platform inspection of study data prior to full export and offline analysis (Figure 4).
text.formatted: CogFlow includes a built-in Analysis module within the researcher portal that is designed to support rapid, in-platform inspection of study data prior to full export and offline analysis (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>).

text.text: The module operates as an on-demand asynchronous report pipeline: a researcher selects a study, specifies an analysis engine (Python or R), and issues a report request; the backend queues a StudyAnalysisReportJob, which a background worker then claims, processes, and resolves against the study's decrypted trial-level records.

The resulting report is generated in multiple output formats simultaneously -Markdown, HTML, PDF, and, when the R engine is selected, an R Markdown document -and stored as versioned StudyAnalysisReportArtifact records that the researcher can subsequently browse or download from the portal.
The report content is structured around a set of configurable report sections.

This includes an overview of run counts and completion status, field-coverage diagnostics summarising which variables were captured and with what density, a numeric summary of behavioural variables of interest computed with descriptive statistics (mean, SD, min, max, and sample size) across all completed runs, and optionally a per-participant summary.

Variable selection is driven by a keyword-matching system seeded with taskfamily defaults (targeting fields such as reaction time, accuracy, correctness, score, and response), which a researcher can override at report-generation time; a priority ranking ensures that core behavioural outcomes appear prominently while configuration-level metadata fields are deprioritised.

A supplementary chart builder, operating separately from the report artifacts, allows researchers to select variables from the report and generate aggregate bar charts with standard-deviation error bars, providing an immediately legible visual impression of the dataset before any data are downloaded.
Together, the report and chart tools are intended to serve early-stage study monitoring rather than replace dedicated statistical software.

Their primary utility is in helping researchers gauge participant engagement, identify obvious data-quality signals, and make informed decisions about whether to continue, adjust, or terminate data collection, all without leaving the platform or decrypting the full result payload locally.

CogFlow integrates natively with two of the most widely used participant recruitment platforms in academic cognitive psychology research, SONA Systems and Prolific Academic, via a dedicated Integrations module in the researcher portal (Figure 5).
text.formatted: CogFlow integrates natively with two of the most widely used participant recruitment platforms in academic cognitive psychology research, SONA Systems and Prolific Academic, via a dedicated Integrations module in the researcher portal (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5</ref>).

text.text: Both integrations follow the same general pattern: the researcher selects a study, configures platform-specific parameters, and the portal generates a complete, ready-to-paste external study URL that embeds the appropriate participant-tracking placeholders.

For SONA, the generated link accepts an optional fixed participant code or leaves the identifier field unpopulated for automatic resolution, and the researcher supplies a SONA completion URL -formatted to the SONA credit-granting web study schema -along with an optional abort URL for incomplete runs; the platform supports the placeholder tokens participant external id, participant key, and run session id in both URLs, enabling automatic credit granting and participantlevel linkage on return from CogFlow.

For Prolific Academic, the portal generates an external study URL that embeds the standard Prolific URL parameters ({{PROLIFIC PID}}, {{STUDY ID}}, and {{SESSION ID}}), with configurable completion behaviour set to auto-redirect to the Prolific completion page by default.

Both link generators are study-scoped and share the same study-selection control, and both support the use of saved study-flow variants for counterbalanced assignment, so researchers running multi-task or counterbalanced designs can configure variant routing once and have recruitment-platform links automatically reflect the correct assignment logic.

Beyond these built-in integrations, the platform's open API and modular link-generation architecture mean that any recruitment system capable of appending URL parameters to an external study link -including institutional custom panels, REDCap-mediated pipelines, or bespoke in-house systems -can be connected without modification to the platform codebase.

CogFlow To Go is a self-contained local deployment mode that allows researchers to run any CogFlow study entirely offline, without a network connection to the platform or any external service, while retaining full compatibility with the same JSON-driven paradigm configurations and data pipeline used in online deployments.

From the portal, a researcher selects a study, configures bundle options, and clicks to prepare and download a bundle archive; the backend assembles the bundle via the StudyTakeToGoBundleView endpoint, packaging the Interpreter runtime together with the study's published configuration JSON and any associated assets into a selfcontained directory that can be unzipped and launched on any target machine (see the UI in Figure 6).

text.text: All CogFlow To Go deployments store data at known destinations.

Interpreter metadata JSONs are stored inside the bundle at a known path (interpreter/metadata/), participant run exports are saved as JSON or CSV files to the browser's default Downloads folder when the debug/download flag is active, and -crucially for laboratory settings -a Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) bridge container is included in the bundle that emits event markers and persists behavioural result files into a local results/ directory via a Docker volume mount, enabling synchronised co-registration with physiological recording systems such as EEG amplifiers.
The bridge is implemented with pylsl, and three LSL system profiles can be selected at bundle-generation time: Generic LSL, BioSemi, and Brain Products.

These profiles have not yet been extensively verified against the corresponding acquisition systems, and full validation of the LSL stream against hardware is planned as part of upcoming laboratory pilot deployments; the current release provides the architectural integration and bundle infrastructure, and empirical characterisation of LSL timing and marker fidelity will be reported in a subsequent communication.

CogFlow's security model is designed around the recognition that participant behavioural data constitutes sensitive research output subject to institutional ethical oversight, and that a platform intended for broad adoption across research groups must provide technically credible data-protection controls that can be directly cited in ethics board submissions and data management plans.
The architecture implements protection at several distinct layers (see the schematic flow of the data governance policies in Figure 7 or at https://cogflow.app/security).
text.formatted: The architecture implements protection at several distinct layers (see the schematic flow of the data governance policies in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">7</ref> or at <ref type="url" target="https://cogflow.app/security">https://cogflow.app/security</ref>).

text.text: At the transport layer, all communication between participant browsers and the platform is conducted exclusively over HTTPS/TLS, preventing interception of in-flight data during the execution of the study or the submission of the results.

At the ingestion layer, result payloads submitted by the Interpreter are encrypted server-side at the point of write, before any persistence to the database, using symmetric Fernet encryption (implemented in security.py) with keys supplied via environment variables and enforced to be non-default in any non-debug deployment; the encrypted ResultEnvelope record is the unit of durable storage, meaning that the underlying behavioral data are never held in plaintext in the database.

Participant identifiers follow a pseudonymisation model: rather than storing raw external identifiers, the backend derives a salted SHA-256 hash of each participant ID at session creation time using a configurable salt value (hash identifier in security.py), so that database records cannot be directly linked to individuals by anyone who does not also hold the salt.

Anonymous launches are supported natively, with the backend generating a random UUID-based identifier for sessions that carry no external participant token, preserving counterbalancing properties across runs while avoiding any linkage risk.
Access to decrypted data is controlled through a multi-factor authorisation pathway.

Researcher access to result payloads requires an authenticated session, role-scoped and organisation-scoped authorisation, and a recent MFA verification window; the decrypt endpoint (POST /api/v1/results/decrypt) enforces these checks server-side on every request and records the outcome -including denied attempts -as an immutable AuditEvent row, capturing actor, action type, target resource, timestamp, and request metadata.

Privileged administrative operations such as role assignment, account deletion, study ownership transfer, and destructive deletions are governed by a formal security matrix requiring authorisation by the platform administrator role, which is reserved for the CogFlow team and never assigned to users, mandatory MFA enrollment, step-up MFA verification with a bounded freshness window, and perpetual audit logging; the matrix is explicitly enforced in the backend handlers rather than relying on frontend route visibility as a control.

The platform's compliance posture is designed to be consistent with the requirements of major research data-governance frameworks, including GDPR (EU 2016/679), UK GDPR, IRB data management plan expectations, and Australian data governance frameworks, with the Ethics and Compliance module inside the researcher portal providing copy-ready paragraphs mapped to specific data-protection dimensions for direct use in ethics board submissions.

The full end-to-end governance flow -from researcher authentication and study configuration through participant submission, server-side encryption, controlled decrypt, audit logging, and retention management -is documented publicly at https://cogflow.app/security, providing transparency suitable for institutional review while not disclosing internal operational details.

text.text: A dedicated probe experiment, run directly in a headed Chromium environment, presented a 300 ms blank inter-trial interval (ITI) followed by a 200 ms stimulus, with a Playwright-dispatched Space keypress fired exactly 100 ms after stimulus onset.
Each session comprised 200 trials (the first 5 discarded as warm-up) and the probe was repeated 20 times, yielding 4,000 measurement trials in total.

Reaction-time precision was taken as the trial-to-trial variability (SD) of recorded response latency, and timer accuracy as the trial-to-trial variability (SD) of the deviation of the measured ITI duration from its nominal 300 ms value; the mean precision index is the average of these two SDs.

Two launch-link profiles were tested -a basic profile representing a standard researcher-authored study link, and a stress profile representing a heavily parameterised configuration -crossed with two network presets: a LAN baseline (no added latency or bandwidth throttling) and a slow 4G simulation (150 ms added latency, 1600 Kbps download, 750 Kbps upload).

text.text: The study-ready interval -the time from navigation start until a usable canvas is first detected in the document object model (DOM) -represents the loading screen and asset initialisation phase that precedes any participant interaction, and is therefore distinct from experiment runtime timing.

Under LAN conditions this initialisation completed in approximately 4.7-4.8 s (both profiles); under slow 4G it extended to approximately 9.2 s, reflecting increased asset transfer time rather than any change in the experiment execution engine itself.

Critically, once the study was underway, frame cadence and input capture latency were effectively invariant across network conditions and launch profiles: the frame interval's 95th percentile (p95) was 16.72-16.73 ms in all four conditions, indicating consistent 60 Hz rendering regardless of connectivity, and synthetic input registration latency averaged 0.10 ms p95 in every condition (Table 3).

text.text: This decoupling of loading-screen duration from runtime timing performance is an important architectural property: participants on slower connections experience a longer wait before the experiment begins, but once the study is running, the software-layer timing of stimulus scheduling and input registration does not differ appreciably from that obtained on a LAN.

The only meaningful runtime degradation observed was an increase in setTimeout scheduling drift under the stress launch profile (timeout p95 ≈ 32 ms vs. ≈ 14-16 ms under basic), a pattern consistent with heightened event-loop pressure rather than frame-rendering instability.

Taken together, these results are consistent with the software-layer timing performance reported for comparable browser-based experimental platforms (Bridges et al., 2020), and support the suitability of CogFlow for online cognitive research where network heterogeneity across participant samples is expected.

In this section, we outline representative usage scenarios for CogFlow's four platform roles: researcher, analyst, instructor, and student.

Although the underlying study infrastructure is shared across all four roles, the platform's permission model governs what each role can author, share, and view, allowing classroom deployments and multi-investigator labs to coexist safely within the same portal.
A fifth, platform administrator role is reserved for the CogFlow team and is never assigned to users; it is therefore not discussed further here.
Table 4 summarises the actions available to each role; the paragraphs below describe how these translate into everyday workflows.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">4</ref> summarises the actions available to each role; the paragraphs below describe how these translate into everyday workflows.

text.text: Researchers represent the platform's primary authoring role and correspond to principal investigators, postdocs, or graduate students running independent projects in cognitive psychology, mathematical psychology, and psychophysics.

A researcher designs a task in the Builder, validates its timing and logic, and publishes it, which creates a study record together with its first configuration version; the resulting participant link can then be distributed directly or routed through a recruitment pipeline such as Prolific.

Because a researcher owns every study they publish, they retain full control over that study's collaborators: access can be granted to, or revoked from, individual co-investigators or analysts, ownership can be reassigned if project staffing changes, and the granularity of what a given collaborator sees, ranging from full per-participant runs down to aggregate summaries only, is set by the owner on a per-collaborator basis.

Analysts occupy a narrower, results-facing role suited to statisticians, research assistants, or external collaborators who need to work with study data without taking on authoring or governance responsibilities.
An analyst cannot create or publish studies; instead, they gain visibility into a study only once its owning researcher explicitly shares it with them.

By default, that shared access is scoped to aggregate-level summaries rather than individual response rows, letting a lab bring in outside collaborators for statistical support while keeping raw, potentially identifying behavioral data restricted to the study owner unless broader access is deliberately granted.
Instructors hold the same authoring privileges as researchers, including designing, validating, publishing, and sharing their own studies, and additionally take on the platform's teaching layer.
From Account Settings, an instructor can create a named course section, which generates a revocable enrollment code and a roster of enrolled students.

Any study a student attaches to that section during publishing automatically grants the instructor a course-collaborator view of that study, so reviewing student work does not require the instructor to individually request or wait for sharing from each student.
This arrangement is deliberately limited to review access: it does not transfer study ownership or give the instructor control over how a student shares that study with anyone else.
Students hold essentially the same study-authoring capabilities as researchers: they can design tasks in the Builder, and validate, publish, and share studies with collaborators of their choosing.

What distinguishes the student role is its tie to coursework: students register with an enrollment code supplied by an instructor, may join additional active sections later from Account Settings, and can optionally attach a published study to the section they belong to.
Attaching a study to a section is what activates the instructor's automatic review access described above, making the student and instructor workflows two halves of the same classroom pipeline.

CogFlow was initially developed to give undergraduate students of Psychology an accessible, GUI-forward environment for designing and running their own experiments without first acquiring programming experience.

As the platform matured, however, its realistic scope of use grew well beyond that original brief: the same Builder-to-Interpreter pipeline that lowers the barrier to entry for coding-averse novice researchers imposes no corresponding ceiling on complexity, and accommodates custom tasks, paradigms, and hardware and software integrations with little additional friction.

CogFlow's intended scope of use is therefore no longer bounded by UX-friendliness for young researchers unfamiliar with stimulus-presentation coding: in current deployment it supports psychophysical, psychological, and cognitive tasks with substantial parameter customisation, spanning both classroom instruction and active multi-investigator lab research, with the platform's role-based permission model (Section 5) allowing both to coexist safely within the same portal.
This dual role, as both a low-friction teaching tool and a capable research instrument, reflects on the incidental universality and widening of the scope of use of CogFlow.

Section 7.2 outlines how the current development roadmap, including expanded paradigm coverage, GUI-based custom task authoring, and further hardware and software integrations, is intended to widen that scope further without raising the barrier to entry for first-time users.
To facilitate user uptake, CogFlow contains a range of tutorials demonstrating many of the platform features described in this paper (see https://cogflow.app/tutorials).

text.text: CogFlow's dual role as an educational tool and a research platform is also a point of difference between it and similar existing platforms.
As Table 1 shows, it is most common for other platforms to offer one or two elements of the experiment deployment pipeline, but not all three elements of building, analysis, and collaboration.

text.text: Those platforms that offer more flexibility in design and deployment are also less often free and open-source.

The most similar platforms to CogFlow in terms of scope and features are https://labvanced.com which offers the same features but requires a paid plan to access some of them, and https://www.psychopy.org + https://pavlovia.org/ which provides the same deployment and collaboration options, but without equivalent analysis tools.

text.text: CogFlow allows educators to guide students through each step of the process of gathering and analysing data within a single platform, and enables research teams to complete primary research securely without requiring multiple platforms or knowledge of multiple coding languages.

Students can also use the knowledge they gained using CogFlow to transition to more advanced research projects, without the need to relearn technical aspects of the experiment building or analysis process.
This places CogFlow in a unique position among equivalent platforms.
Two complementary lines of development are planned for CogFlow's paradigm library.

The first extends the platform's existing continuous-presentation engine, already used for paradigms such as Continuous Image Presentation (CIP) and Security Operations Center Dashboard (SOC-dashboard) scheduling, to support more complex and genuinely multi-task presentation designs, in which several concurrently running subtasks with independent timing and overlapping presentation windows can be composed and scheduled within a single study rather than authored as bespoke, one-off plugins.

The second runs in the opposite direction of complexity: expanding the built-in library of classical paradigms (e.g., Posner cueing, Garner interference, Navon global/local task, among others) so that researchers who need a validated, ready-to-use implementation of an established manipulation are not required to rebuild it from primitives, lowering the effort required to include a standard task within a larger study.
A further planned addition is an editable authoring surface for the existing "Custom" task type.

At present, bespoke paradigms are added to CogFlow in one of two ways: researchers may develop a jsPsych plugin themselves and contribute it through the GitHub repository, or commission the CogFlow development team to build a task tailored to their experiment.

The planned extension is intended for researchers already familiar with jsPsych (de Leeuw et al., 2023) who wish to write plugin-level task logic directly within the Builder's GUI, retaining the platform's configuration versioning, JSON export, and deployment infrastructure for tasks that the built-in library does not yet cover.

text.text: Software and hardware integration work is planned on two further fronts.

On the data-acquisition side, this includes Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) compatibility with multiple EEG acquisition systems and software products, with possible expansion into other neuroscientific data modalities, building on the pylsl bridge already included in CogFlow To Go (Section 2.6) toward validated, hardware-synchronised data collection.

On the curricular side, this includes "out-of-the-box" educational modules built around common course components in university-based Psychology, Cognitive Science, and Neuroscience programmes at both the undergraduate and graduate level, intended to let instructors deploy a validated teaching exercise (for example, a standard demonstration paradigm together with an accompanying analysis walkthrough) without first assembling it themselves in the Builder.
